front: What is the difference between `>` and `>>`?
back: `>` creates the file or replaces it (it empties it first); `>>` appends to the end. `>` has no “are you sure?”, so it can silently destroy data.

front: Which stream numbers do stdin, stdout and stderr have?
back: stdin is 0, stdout is 1 and stderr is 2. Plain `>` is short for `1>`, so it never catches error messages.

front: Mira wants only the error messages of `make` in `err.txt`. Which command?
back: `make 2> err.txt`. `2>` redirects stream 2 (stderr); normal output still appears on the screen.

front: How do you send both stdout and stderr of `ls nothere build.log` into `both.txt`?
back: `ls nothere build.log > both.txt 2>&1` (or bash’s short form `&>`). `2>&1` means “send stream 2 where stream 1 goes”.

front: Why does `ls nothere 2>&1 > out.txt` still show the error on the screen?
back: The shell reads left to right: stream 2 is first pointed where stream 1 is now (the screen), and only then stream 1 moves to the file. Write `> out.txt 2>&1`.

front: What does `command 2> /dev/null` do?
back: It throws the error messages away. `/dev/null` swallows everything written to it and always reads as empty.

front: What does `wc -l < build.log` do differently from `wc -l build.log`?
back: `<` lets the shell feed the file into stdin, so `wc` prints only the number. With the file name as an argument, `wc` prints the name too.

front: What is the difference between `|` and `>`?
back: `|` connects one command’s stdout to another command’s stdin. `>` sends stdout into a file. `ls | file.txt` is an error, because `file.txt` isn’t a command.

front: Which pipeline counts the lines containing `ERROR` in `build.log`?
back: `grep ERROR build.log | wc -l`. Each stage does one small job, and `wc -l` answers “how many?”.

front: Does a pipe carry error messages from the left-hand command?
back: No, only stdout. Errors still go to the screen unless you add `2>&1` to the left-hand command.

front: What does `tee errors.txt` do in `grep ERROR build.log | tee errors.txt | wc -l`?
back: `tee` copies its input into `errors.txt` and also passes it on, so you save the matching lines and still count them.

front: Which command shows the last 20 lines of `/var/log/syslog`, and which shows the first 3 lines of `build.log`?
back: `tail -n 20 /var/log/syslog` and `head -n 3 build.log`. Both show 10 lines by default.

front: What does `wc` print without options, and which options pick one count?
back: Lines, words and bytes, in that order. `-l` counts lines, `-w` words and `-c` bytes.

front: A long log doesn’t fit on the screen. Which command lets you page through it, and how do you search and quit?
back: `less build.log`. Type `/word` to search forward, `n` for the next match, Space for the next page and `q` to quit.

front: Why does `sort` put `1100` before `700`, and how do you fix it?
back: Without options `sort` compares text, and `1` comes before `7`. Add `-n` for a numeric sort; `-r` reverses the order.

front: What do `-t,` and `-k3` mean in `sort -t, -k3 -n playtest.csv`?
back: `-t,` makes the comma the field separator and `-k3` sorts by the third field. `-n` compares it as a number.

front: Which command prints the first and third comma-separated fields of `playtest.csv`?
back: `cut -d, -f1,3 playtest.csv`. `-d` sets the delimiter and `-f` picks the fields. The default delimiter is a Tab, not a comma.

front: Why does `uniq` often fail to remove all duplicates, and what do you run first?
back: `uniq` only collapses neighbouring duplicate lines. Run `sort` first: `sort names.txt | uniq`. `uniq -c` adds the count in front of each line.

front: What do `grep -i`, `-v` and `-c` do?
back: `-i` ignores case, `-v` prints the lines that do not match and `-c` prints only the number of matching lines.

front: Which options of `grep` show line numbers and search a directory tree?
back: `-n` puts the line number before each match, and `-r` searches every file below a directory, prefixing matches with the file name.

front: In a regular expression, what do `.` and `*` mean?
back: `.` is any one character, and `*` means the item before it repeated zero or more times. So `.*` means “anything”. Don’t confuse this with file globs, where `*` alone is “anything”.

front: What does `grep '^[sb]' enemies.txt` match?
back: Lines that start with `s` or `b`. `^` anchors the start of the line and `[sb]` is one character out of the set, case-sensitive.

front: What do `[a-z]` and `[^0-9]` match?
back: `[a-z]` is one character from the range, and `[^0-9]` is one character that is not a digit. The `^` inside brackets negates the set.

front: How do `^` and `$` differ when used in `grep`?
back: `^` matches the start of the line and `$` the end. `grep 't$'` finds lines that end with `t`.

front: What does `grep -E 'ghosts?'` match, and why does plain `grep 'ghosts?'` find nothing?
back: `-E` enables extended regular expressions, where `?` makes the `s` optional, so `ghost` and `ghosts` match. Plain `grep` treats `?` as a literal question mark.

front: Which command finds lines containing either `bat` or `ghost`?
back: `grep -E 'bat|ghost' enemies.txt`. In extended syntax `|` means “or”. Quote the pattern so the shell doesn’t treat the `|` as a pipe.

front: What does `+` mean in `grep -E 'ro+t'`?
back: One or more of the previous item, so it matches `rot`, `root` and `rooot`. `?` is zero or one, and `*` is zero or more.

front: On exam 010-160, how do you write an optional `s` with plain `grep`, as in `ghost` or `ghosts`?
back: `grep 'ghosts\?'`. In basic regular expressions GNU `grep` needs a backslash for `?`; a bare `?` is just a question mark. `.`, `[ ]` and `*` need no backslash.

front: What does `grep 'go*blin'` match, using basic regular expressions?
back: `gblin`, `goblin`, `gooblin` and so on: `o*` means zero or more `o`. The `*` works in basic syntax without a backslash.
